blocks.text: An is-a claim is a design judgment supported by behavioral compatibility, not just grammar. A derived class that refuses ordinary base operations or weakens their safety guarantees can violate clients’ expectations even though the compiler accepts the hierarchy. Keep base interfaces small and meaningful rather than using inheritance as an unrestricted bucket of reusable implementation.
rich: An is-a claim is a design judgment supported by behavioral compatibility, not just grammar. A derived class that refuses ordinary base operations or weakens their safety guarantees can violate clients’ expectations even though the compiler accepts the hierarchy. Keep base interfaces small and meaningful rather than using inheritance as an unrestricted bucket of reusable implementation.

blocks.text: An is-a relationship should support substitution under the base interface’s stated contract. A sensor can be a device when every operation exposed as a device remains meaningful for a sensor. Inheriting from a class solely to obtain storage or helper methods does not establish that relationship. Composition is often clearer when the intended statement is “this object uses a device configuration” rather than “this object is a device.”
rich: An is-a relationship should support substitution under the base interface’s stated contract. A sensor can be a device when every operation exposed as a device remains meaningful for a sensor. Inheriting from a class solely to obtain storage or helper methods does not establish that relationship. Composition is often clearer when the intended statement is “this object uses a device configuration” rather than “this object is a device.”

blocks.text: Substitution includes failure and state rules. If a base operation promises to accept every nonnegative sample, a derived implementation that rejects half those samples without a documented reason narrows the contract. If the base promises a read-only query, a derived implementation that changes external state may surprise callers even though it has the same function signature. The compiler checks type compatibility, not every behavioral promise.

blocks.text: Public inheritance exposes a derived-to-base relationship to callers. Private inheritance instead restricts that relationship and is more often an implementation technique. This book uses public inheritance for explicit interfaces and composition for ordinary has-a relationships; it does not require a class hierarchy merely because several classes share an integer or string member.

blocks.text: A useful design test is to write a small function that knows only the base interface. Can it operate on every proposed derived type without special-case downcasts or name checks? Frequent questions such as “which derived type is this really?” can indicate that the base abstraction is missing an operation or that the hierarchy is modeling unrelated concepts.

topics.title: 8.1.2 Controlling Member Accessibility
topics.summary: Public, protected, and private access determine which code can name members through the relevant language rules. The scale is protected in this teaching example so the derived sensor can use it directly. That choice visibly couples the derived class to the base representation.

blocks.text: In a production design, a protected query or composed calibration object may preserve more freedom than a protected writable field. Derived code should not casually bypass an invariant established by the base. Private inheritance and protected inheritance have different interface implications; they are not needed merely to demonstrate basic specialization here.

blocks.text: Access control is about which code can name and use members. A derived class can access protected base members under the language’s rules, while ordinary callers cannot access them directly. That does not mean protected mutable data is well encapsulated. Every derived class that can write a protected field participates in maintaining the base’s invariant.
rich: Access control is about which code can name and use members. A derived class can access protected base members under the language’s rules, while ordinary callers cannot access them directly. That does not mean protected mutable data is well encapsulated. Every derived class that can write a protected field participates in maintaining the base’s invariant.

blocks.text: Suppose the base stores a positive calibration scale. Making the scale protected allows a derived class to assign zero or a negative value unless all derived code follows the rule. A protected operation that validates changes can preserve a narrower interface. Better still, a private immutable value can eliminate mutation when the application does not need it. Choose access based on required behavior, not on the idea that derived classes deserve unrestricted access to every detail.

Choose access based on required behavior, not on the idea that derived classes deserve unrestricted access to every detail.

blocks.text: A public getter can expose a representation without allowing mutation, but it can also make callers depend on that representation. Decide whether the useful public concept is a raw scale or an operation such as calibrate. An interface that exposes only the required behavior gives the implementation more freedom to change later.

topics.title: 8.2 Understanding Construction Through Inheritance Hierarchies
topics.summary: A derived object includes its base subobjects. Those bases must be constructed before the derived constructor body uses them, and they remain until after the derived destructor body finishes. Understanding that order prevents calling behavior that assumes a not-yet-ready or already-ended derived state.

blocks.text: Base subobjects are initialized before the derived class’s own members and constructor body. Non-static data members are initialized in their declaration order, not the order in which they happen to appear in an initializer list. The order matters when one member’s initialization depends on another or when a later stage can throw.

The order matters when one member’s initialization depends on another or when a later stage can throw.

blocks.text: For the sensor, the base constructor records its event first. The derived constructor records its event after the base has completed. At that point, base state is available for the derived initialization. A base constructor must not assume the final derived object’s complete state already exists. Virtual calls during construction follow special rules tied to the currently constructing class; Chapter 9 explains why relying on derived overrides from base construction is a common design error.

blocks.text: Failure also follows the completed-subobject boundary. If the derived constructor throws, the already constructed base and members are destroyed. The destructor of the incomplete derived object does not run. A resource that needs cleanup should therefore live in a completed owning member or base subobject, not depend on a cleanup body that construction never reaches.

Deleting a derived object through an owning base pointer would be invalid for this design, so the example never does that. Chapter 9 provides a virtual destructor for a polymorphic ownership interface. Do not copy the nonvirtual destructor into a base that clients will use for polymorphic deletion.

blocks.text: Destruction reverses the completed object’s composition: the derived destructor body runs, then its members are destroyed in reverse declaration order, then base subobjects are destroyed in the appropriate reverse order. This lets outer behavior release its own responsibilities before the underlying base machinery disappears. Borrowed services used during destruction must still be alive at that point.

blocks.text: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer requires an appropriate destruction design. For an ordinary polymorphic base intended for public deletion, a virtual destructor is the usual solution. A non-polymorphic base can instead prohibit that use, for example through a protected destructor when suitable. The example simply never performs base-pointer deletion; it should not be copied into a factory returning owning base pointers without revisiting the interface.

Their interfaces and destruction policies are not a promise that they are intended as your runtime-polymorphic base classes. A wrapper containing a vector can expose selected operations without making every container operation part of the new domain type’s contract.

topics.title: Failure clinic — The initializer list that looked ordered
topics.summary: A class lists one member before another in its initializer list, but declares them in the opposite order. The programmer assumes the visual list controls initialization and reads a member that has not yet been initialized. A warning can reveal the mismatch, but the durable repair is to arrange declarations and dependencies intentionally, then write the initializer list in that same order for clarity.

topics.title: Review and solution reasoning
topics.summary: Inheritance supplies a type relationship and subobject structure, not behavioral correctness automatically. Declaration order controls member initialization. Completed subobjects clean up when later construction fails. A borrowed observer must outlive the events it records. Base-pointer ownership requires a destruction policy designed for that use, not merely a modern-looking smart pointer.
